Abstract:

The present research focuses on the development of next-generation medium manganese steel (MMnS) with enhanced mechanical and wear behaviour through controlled alloy design and optimized thermomechanical processing routes. Medium manganese steels, a category of the third generation advanced high-strength steels (AHSS), typically contain 3-12 wt.% Mn and are considered as the promising candidates in the field of automotive engineering. These steels offer an excellent balance of strength-ductility and are comparatively cheaper than second-generation high-Mn and Hadfield steel. However, several incumbent steels currently used in automotive panels express insufficient impact energy absorption properties, resulting in catastrophic failure during collisions. Likewise, these steels are also not effectively used to fabricate various automotive components, such as gears, engines, and pistons, due to their moderate wear resistance. Therefore, a strategic approach is adopted in the present work through alloying addition, thermomechanical processing and surface treatment to modify both the mechanical and tribological performance of the developed alloy.

The current approach critically addresses the persistent knowledge gaps in understanding the complex interplay between the processing parameters and alloying elements on microstructure evolution and mechanical performance. It systematically investigates the role of alloying elements, such as Mn, Cr, Ni, Al and RE on retained austenite stability, activation of TRIP/TWIP mechanism, and the corresponding strength-ductility balance and wear behaviour across different grades of medium manganese steel.
